description_ru: Почему антибиотики теряют силу и как это связано с естественным отбором, плазмидами и фермерскими практиками? Разбираем механизм устойчивости бактерий.
text:
In 1945, while accepting his Nobel Prize for the discovery of penicillin, Alexander Fleming ended his lecture with a warning that sounds uncomfortably modern. The danger, he said, was that careless people would under-dose themselves, exposing microbes to quantities of the drug too small to kill them, and thereby teach them to resist it. Eight decades later, his prediction has become one of the central problems in medicine.

To see why resistance is almost inevitable, it helps to think about the sheer scale of bacterial populations. A single teaspoon of infected tissue can contain billions of cells, and under favourable conditions a bacterium such as Escherichia coli can divide roughly every twenty minutes. Whenever DNA is copied, occasional errors creep in. Most of these mutations are harmless or harmful to the cell, but in a population that large, a few will, purely by chance, alter the target of an antibiotic or help the cell pump the drug out before it can act.

The drugs themselves work in different ways. Penicillin and its relatives interfere with the construction of the bacterial cell wall, so that growing cells burst, while others, such as tetracyclines, jam the ribosomes that manufacture proteins. Each mechanism offers bacteria a different route to evasion. Crucially, the antibiotic does not cause such mutations. It merely reveals them. When a course of treatment begins, the susceptible majority dies, and the rare cells with some natural tolerance survive and multiply into the space left behind. This is natural selection in its purest form, observable within days rather than millennia. The more often and the more widely antibiotics are used, the stronger the selective pressure becomes, and the faster the resistant minority takes over.

A striking demonstration came in 2016, when researchers at Harvard and the Technion built a giant rectangular dish, roughly the size of a tray, with bands of agar containing no antibiotic at the edges and a thousand times the lethal dose in the middle. They seeded harmless bacteria at the edges and filmed the result. At first the colonies stalled at the first band of drug. Then one lineage found a mutation and advanced, and another followed, each step opening a path to the next, until within about ten days the bacteria were thriving in a concentration that would once have killed them outright. Evolution, normally invisible, had been turned into a time-lapse film.

Mutation is only half the story. Bacteria also swap genes with one another, a process called horizontal gene transfer, and they do so with a casualness that would astonish a geneticist working on animals. Small rings of DNA known as plasmids can carry several resistance genes at once and pass between cells, and even between different species, by direct contact. A harmless gut bacterium can therefore hand a dangerous relative the equivalent of a skeleton key. This is why resistance to a drug can appear in a hospital in one continent and show up, months later, in another.

The consequences are already measurable. A major study published in The Lancet in 2022 estimated that drug-resistant bacterial infections were directly responsible for about 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019, and were associated with nearly five million. That puts them in the same league as HIV and malaria. Familiar names have become shorthand for the trend: MRSA, or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, first appeared in hospitals within two years of methicillin's introduction in 1959, and has since spread into communities, while certain strains of tuberculosis now respond to almost none of the standard drugs. Routine procedures such as caesarean sections, joint replacements and chemotherapy depend on effective antibiotics to prevent infection, so their loss would quietly undermine much of modern surgery.

Agriculture plays a large part. In many countries, a considerable share of antibiotics is given to livestock, sometimes to promote growth rather than to treat illness. Resistant bacteria can then pass to people through food, water or direct contact. Several regions, including the European Union, have now banned the use of antibiotics as growth promoters, and in some places, resistance in farm animals has begun to decline, which is encouraging evidence that policy can make a difference.

Meanwhile, the pipeline of new drugs has thinned, a worrying development given that remarkably few entirely new classes of antibiotic have reached patients in recent decades, and most new approvals are variations on older themes. Developing an antibiotic is expensive, and because the best new ones are held in reserve for the most severe infections, they earn little money compared with a drug taken daily for a chronic condition. Many large companies have therefore withdrawn from the field. Researchers are exploring alternatives, among them bacteriophages, which are viruses that infect only bacteria, and compounds discovered by machine-learning systems that screen millions of molecules. In 2020, one such programme identified a promising new antibiotic, named halicin, which was effective against several resistant strains in laboratory tests.

Optimism is justified, but only up to a point. No single invention will resolve the problem, because bacteria will adapt to anything we use against them. The sustainable response is a combination of stewardship and prevention: prescribing antibiotics only when they are really needed, completing prescribed courses, improving hygiene and sanitation, developing vaccines that prevent infections to begin with, and monitoring resistance patterns globally. None of this is glamorous. Yet it is precisely this quiet discipline that may decide whether a scratch on a child's knee remains trivial for the next century, as it has been for the last eighty years.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: inˈevitable, susˈceptible, horiˈzontal. В длинных словах слоги после ударного быстро сокращайте.
В служебных словах the, that, therefore звонкое «ð»: язык между зубами, голос включён.
Звук «æ» широкий, рот открыт: plasmids, can. Не заменяйте на «э».
Дифтонг «aɪ»: от открытого «а» к краткому «и»: time, microbes — звук не обрывать.

questions.question: What warning did Fleming give in 1945?
questions.answer: That under-dosing with penicillin would teach microbes to resist it.

questions.question: How do resistant bacteria become common?
questions.answer: Antibiotics kill susceptible cells, so naturally tolerant mutants survive and multiply.

questions.question: What is horizontal gene transfer?
questions.answer: Bacteria swapping genes, often on plasmids, even between species.

questions.question: Name one way to slow resistance.
questions.answer: Prescribing antibiotics only when needed, hygiene, vaccines or new alternatives like phages.
